\chapter{Things You Ask For}
\label{ch:te-ask-for}
\hlchaptermodality{46}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five everyday things I might ask someone for in Telugu, and say which of them Telugu has always had and which arrived from elsewhere.}

Complete TE-C46-book and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[paṇḍu]{\te{పండు} (paṇḍu) — a fruit}

\label{lesson:TE-C46-fruit}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{bhārya} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{పండు}}
\textbf{\te{పండు}} (\emph{paṇḍu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a fruit\textquotedblright{}.

\te{పండు} is also a verb: \emph{to ripen}. The fruit is named for what happened to it — the ripened thing — and Telugu never troubled to invent a second noun. Say \emph{paṇḍu} of a mango on the table and you mean the fruit; say it of the tree's crop and you mean it is coming ripe.

Kannada writes the same inherited word \ka{ಹಣ್ಣು} (\emph{haṇṇu}). That \emph{p-} at the front turning into \emph{h-} is a regular Kannada sound law, and it has already turned up once, on \te{పాలు} beside \ka{ಹಾಲು}. Watch for it again.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things you might ask someone for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{paṇḍu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{paṇḍu}, then \emph{dayacēsi paṇḍu ivvaṇḍi} — \textquotedblleft{}please give a fruit\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{పండు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a fruit\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[baṭṭa]{\te{బట్ట} (baṭṭa) — cloth}

\label{lesson:TE-C46-cloth}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{paṇḍu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{బట్ట}}
\textbf{\te{బట్ట}} (\emph{baṭṭa}) — \textquotedblleft{}cloth\textquotedblright{}.

\te{బట్ట} is the plain word for cloth: the bolt on the shelf, the washing on the line, the rag in your hand.

Sanskrit has \emph{paṭṭa}, \textquotedblleft{}a strip of cloth, a bandage\textquotedblright{}, and here the borrowing most likely ran the unusual way — out of Dravidian and into Sanskrit, rather than the other direction this book has shown so often. The same strip reached English by a different road: Hindi \emph{paṭṭī}, a wrapping, is the soldier's \emph{puttee}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: a fruit and a cloth.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{baṭṭa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{paṇḍu}, then \emph{baṭṭa}, and ask for each one with \emph{dayacēsi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{బట్ట} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}cloth\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dīpaṁ]{\te{దీపం} (dīpaṁ) — a lamp}

\label{lesson:TE-C46-lamp}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{baṭṭa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{దీపం}}
\textbf{\te{దీపం}} (\emph{dīpaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a lamp\textquotedblright{}.

\te{దీపం} is the small clay lamp with oil and a wick. Its Sanskrit root \emph{dīp} means \textquotedblleft{}to blaze\textquotedblright{}, so the word names the burning rather than the vessel.

Put \te{దీప} together with a word meaning \textquotedblleft{}a row\textquotedblright{} and you get \emph{dīpāvaḷi}, \textquotedblleft{}a row of lamps\textquotedblright{} — the festival English spells Diwali. The ending is the tatsama neuter \textbf{-\te{ం}}, the same shape already carried by \te{హృదయం} and \te{భోజనం}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: a fruit, a cloth, a lamp.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dīpaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all three, then name the one that came in from Sanskrit
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{దీపం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a lamp\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[uppu]{\te{ఉప్పు} (uppu) — salt}

\label{lesson:TE-C46-salt}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{dīpaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ఉప్పు}}
\textbf{\te{ఉప్పు}} (\emph{uppu}) — \textquotedblleft{}salt\textquotedblright{}.

Proto-Dravidian had \textbf{*uppu}, and the whole family kept it almost untouched: Tamil \ta{உப்பு}, Kannada \ka{ಉಪ್ಪು}, Malayalam \ml{ഉപ്പ്}. A word this ordinary gives nobody a reason to replace it.

Notice the doubled \te{ప్ప} in the middle. Telugu likes a consonant twice inside a short word — \te{కుక్క}, \te{పిల్లి}, \te{కన్ను} all do it — and the doubling is not decoration: it is the difference between one word and another.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four. Three of them inherited, one borrowed.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{uppu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all four in order, then say which one has not changed in three thousand years
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{ఉప్పు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}salt\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pustakaṁ]{\te{పుస్తకం} (pustakaṁ) — a book}

\label{lesson:TE-C46-book}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{uppu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{పుస్తకం}}
\textbf{\te{పుస్తకం}} (\emph{pustakaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a book\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{pustaka} is the source, but the trail behind it leaves India altogether. Middle Persian \emph{post} meant \textquotedblleft{}hide, skin\textquotedblright{} — the thing written on before paper.

So the Telugu word for a book carries an animal skin folded up inside it, and it arrived by the same north-western road as \te{రోజు}, which turned out to be Persian too. Two of these five walked in from outside; three were always here.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five things you might ask for: a fruit, a cloth, a lamp, salt, a book.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pustakaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then sort them into the inherited and the borrowed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{పుస్తకం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a book\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
